note: Oxygen pulls shared electrons closer, giving water's bent shape and its polarity — the reason water is such a good solvent.
Nitrogen shares one electron pair with each of three hydrogens, leaving a lone pair that makes ammonia a base.
Carbon and hydrogen have nearly equal electronegativity, so each C–H bond is only weakly polar overall.
Chlorine is far more electronegative than hydrogen, pulling the shared pair toward itself and making HCl a strong acid in water.
Fluorine is the most electronegative element, making this one of the most polarized single bonds possible.
A single shared pair, pulled toward the more electronegative bromine atom.
A single shared pair; the small electronegativity gap makes this one of the weaker hydrogen halides.
Structurally similar to water but with a smaller electronegativity gap, so it's a weaker, smellier analog.
Each C=O bond is polar, but the two point in opposite directions, so the linear molecule cancels out to nonpolar overall.
A reddish-brown gas; nitrogen and oxygen also form NO and N2O4 depending on conditions.
A pungent gas from burning sulfur; further oxidation under industrial conditions produces SO3 for making sulfuric acid.
Phosphorus shares three pairs with chlorine; with excess chlorine it can react further to form PCl5.
Not a small molecule — silicon and oxygen link into a giant covalent lattice. This is ordinary quartz sand.
A giant covalent lattice nearly as hard as diamond, used industrially as an abrasive (carborundum).
Each C–Cl bond is polar, but the symmetric tetrahedral shape cancels the polarity, making the molecule nonpolar overall.
Boron has only three valence electrons to share, leaving it electron-deficient — BF3 is a classic Lewis acid.
Best known as hydrogen cyanide; carbon and nitrogen share a triple bond within the molecule.
Ordinary rust. Iron also forms FeO (iron(II) oxide) under different conditions — iron's oxidation state varies.
Iron(III) chloride. Iron also commonly forms FeCl2 (iron(II) chloride).
Copper(II) oxide, a black solid. Copper also forms the red Cu2O (copper(I) oxide).
Copper(II) chloride, a blue-green solid often used to color flames.
Nickel(II) oxide, a green-black solid used in ceramics and battery electrodes.
Cobalt(II) chloride — famous for changing color with humidity, from blue (dry) to pink (hydrated).
Manganese(IV) oxide, used in dry-cell batteries and as a catalyst for decomposing hydrogen peroxide.
Chromium(III) oxide, a green pigment and the compound behind chromium's corrosion resistance.
Titanium dioxide, the most widely used white pigment, also found in sunscreen and paint.
Tin(IV) oxide, used in ceramic glazes and as a transparent conductive coating.
Lead(IV) oxide, the electrode material in lead-acid car batteries.
Mercury(II) oxide, a toxic red or yellow solid, historically used in early batteries.
Gold(III) chloride — gold's normal reluctance to react is overcome by chlorine's strong pull on electrons.
Platinum(II) chloride, a starting material for making other platinum compounds and catalysts.
Tungsten trioxide, a yellow solid used in electrochromic 'smart glass' that darkens electrically.
Lead(II) sulfide — the mineral galena, historically used as an early semiconductor crystal detector.
One of the few real noble-gas compounds — xenon is large enough for its outer electrons to be coaxed into bonding with fluorine.
A rare, explosively unstable noble-gas compound, showing xenon can be forced to share electrons under the right conditions.
Krypton bonds even more reluctantly than xenon; KrF2 only survives at very low temperatures.
